content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that organizations previously relying on posting PDF versions of immunization schedules on their websites adopt a safer and more efficient method known as content syndication. This approach ensures that the most up-to-date and accurate immunization schedule information is consistently displayed on their websites. By embedding two lines of CDC-provided code into their web pages, organizations can automatically load the current immunization schedules and footnotes directly from the CDC. This method guarantees that any updates or revisions made by the CDC are immediately reflected on the organization's website without requiring additional manual updates. The schedules are seamlessly integrated into the website's existing design, leaving other images and navigation elements unchanged. Additionally, organizations can offer downloadable PDFs of the schedules, allowing staff and visitors to print and view the most current versions confidently. The CDC provides technical assistance to organizations implementing this content syndication method. For support, organizations can complete an email form on the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases (NCIRD) web support page, and a member of the NCIRD web team will provide assistance. Each year, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) reviews and updates the recommended immunization schedules for individuals aged 0 through 18 years to ensure they align with current recommendations for licensed vaccines. In October 2012, ACIP approved the 2013 immunization schedules, which included several changes from the 2012 schedules. Healthcare providers are advised to use both the recommended schedule and the catch-up schedule in conjunction with their accompanying footnotes for comprehensive guidance. These schedules are available in various formats, including printable versions in landscape and pocket-sized designs, as well as laminated options. A parent-friendly version of the regular schedule is also available. For 2013, new references and links to additional information were added, including travel vaccine requirements and recommendations. Updates also included guidance for vaccinating individuals with primary and secondary immunodeficiencies. Changes to the schedules included combining the previously separate schedules for ages 0–6 years and 7–18 years into a single Recommended Immunization Schedule for Persons Aged 0 Through 18 Years. Additional wording was added to clarify vaccine dose numbers in series, and the meningococcal conjugate vaccine (MCV4) schedule was updated to reflect the licensure of the Hib-MenCY vaccine for infants as young as six weeks. For individuals who fall behind or start late, catch-up vaccination should be administered at the earliest opportunity, as indicated by the green bars in the catch-up schedule. Minimum intervals between doses are provided in the catch-up schedule. School entry and adolescent vaccine age groups are highlighted in bold. The catch-up schedule ensures that vaccine series do not need to be restarted, regardless of the time elapsed between doses. The footnotes accompanying the immunization schedules provide additional guidance on vaccine use, including contraindications and precautions. For example, the hepatitis B vaccine should be administered to all newborns before hospital discharge, with specific recommendations for infants born to hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg)-positive mothers. Rotavirus vaccines are recommended for all infants, with specific schedules for RV1 and RV5 vaccines. Catch-up vaccination for rotavirus has age-specific limitations, and the maximum age for the final dose is eight months. The ACIP also annually reviews and updates the adult immunization schedule, summarizing existing recommendations for routine vaccine use in adults. The 2013 adult schedule incorporated changes to vaccine recommendations, including the use of the 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) for adults aged 19 years and older with immunocompromising conditions, functional or anatomic asplenia, cerebrospinal fluid leaks, or cochlear implants. The timing of PCV13 administration relative to the 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) was clarified. Adults with certain medical conditions are recommended to receive two doses of PPSV23 before age 65, with an additional dose at age 65 if at least five years have passed since the last dose. For tetanus, diphtheria, and acellular pertussis (Tdap) vaccine, recommendations were expanded to include routine vaccination of adults aged 65 years and older and pregnant women during each pregnancy, ideally between 27 and 36 weeks' gestation. This recommendation aims to optimize protection for both the pregnant woman and her infant during the first few months of life when the infant is at highest risk for severe pertussis-related illness and death. The live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) was updated to include a quadrivalent formulation containing two influenza B virus strains. Beginning with the 2013–14 influenza season, only the quadrivalent LAIV formulation is expected to be available. The abbreviation for inactivated influenza vaccine (IIV) was updated to reflect both trivalent and quadrivalent formulations. Additional updates were made to footnotes for vaccines such as measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR); human papillomavirus (HPV); zoster; hepatitis A; and hepatitis B. For example, the MMR footnote was modified to clarify that a provider diagnosis of measles, mumps, or rubella is no longer considered acceptable evidence of immunity. The HPV footnote was updated to include information on vaccination during pregnancy, and the zoster footnote clarified that vaccination is recommended for individuals aged 60 years and older, regardless of prior herpes zoster episodes. The meningococcal vaccine recommendations were updated to include two doses of meningococcal conjugate vaccine (MCV4) for adults with functional asplenia or persistent complement component deficiencies, as well as for HIV-infected individuals. A single dose of meningococcal vaccine is recommended for microbiologists routinely exposed to Neisseria meningitidis, military recruits, and travelers to areas with hyperendemic or epidemic meningococcal disease. First-year college students living in residence halls should also be vaccinated if they have not received a dose on or after their 16th birthday. Contraindications and precautions for vaccine administration were clarified. For example, individuals with a history of severe allergic reactions (e.g., anaphylaxis) to a vaccine component or a previous dose should not receive the vaccine. Moderate or severe acute illness with or without fever is a precaution for vaccination. Pregnancy was removed as a precaution for hepatitis A vaccination, as it is an inactivated vaccine and recommended for individuals with high-risk conditions. Healthcare providers are reminded to consult the full ACIP vaccine recommendations and package inserts for additional information on vaccine-related contraindications, precautions, and excipients. Adverse events following vaccination should be reported to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS). The immunization schedules are approved by professional organizations such as the American Academy of Family Physicians, the American College of Physicians, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the American College of Nurse-Midwives.
